title: Running late
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in a GP practice. Your morning surgery is running 40 minutes late, and the waiting room is full.

Reception messages you that the mother of a two-year-old has phoned asking for a call back today. The message just says "worried about son", and the receptionist didn't ask any more. The practice's duty doctor handles urgent same-day requests, but has a long list today.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 4 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Tell reception you'll call her at the end of surgery.
options.brief: Could leave an unwell child waiting for over an hour.
options.detailed: Calling after surgery is fine for routine queries, but you don't yet know whether this is routine, and a young child can deteriorate quickly.

options.text: Ask the duty doctor to call her back.
options.brief: Appropriate for urgent requests, though it adds to a busy colleague's list without knowing the urgency.
options.detailed: The duty doctor exists for urgent same-day requests, so this is reasonable. It ranks second because the duty doctor is also busy, and a brief call from you would establish whether it's urgent at all.

options.text: Ask reception to call her back and find out more about her son's symptoms.
options.brief: Reception can gather details, but judging urgency needs a clinician.
options.detailed: Receptionists can collect useful information, and some practices use trained care navigators. But deciding how urgent a young child's symptoms are is a clinical judgement, so relying on this may delay the right response.

options.text: Call the mother back briefly before your next patient.
options.brief: A short call tells you how urgent it is, and young children can deteriorate quickly.
options.detailed: "Worried about son" could be anything from a rash to a very unwell child, and only a clinician can judge which. A brief call lets you assess urgency directly and then deal with it, bring the child in, or arrange a later call. It makes you a little later, but it is the safest option.

explanation.issue: This tests how you prioritise an unclear request about a young child when you're already behind.
explanation.keyDetails: The message is vague, and reception didn't ask more. The child is two. You are 40 minutes behind, and the duty doctor is busy.
explanation.reasoning: [D] assesses urgency quickly and directly, [B] uses the practice's urgent system, and [C] gathers information but without clinical judgement. [A] could delay care for an unwell child.
explanation.competing: Some would ask the duty doctor first, as that is their role. The key prefers a brief call yourself because it takes a few minutes and avoids adding to a busy colleague's list before you know whether it's urgent.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 1, prioritising patients according to clinical need.
